## Two follow-up questions in Rivera's hiring study {.transcript-slide}

<div class="cols"><div class="transcript"><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Interviewer:</span> Tell me about a recent candidate who seemed like a good fit for the firm.</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Evaluator:</span> The conversation flowed. We had a surprising amount in common.</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Interviewer:</span> What did you find you had in common?</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Evaluator:</span> We had both rowed in college and talked about long training days.</div></div><div class="transcript"><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Interviewer:</span> Tell me about a recent candidate who seemed like a good fit for the firm.</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Evaluator:</span> The conversation flowed. We had a surprising amount in common.</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Interviewer:</span> So their background matched the firm's culture?</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Evaluator:</span> Yes, I suppose so.</div></div></div>

<div class="citation">Instructor-written comparison based on Rivera (2012), “Hiring as Cultural Matching,” <em>American Sociological Review</em> 77(6): 999–1022.</div>

---

## Why the first probe is more useful

<div class="cols"><div><h3>First probe</h3><p>It asks the evaluator to explain what “in common” meant in this case.</p><p>The answer gives us a concrete comparison that we can examine.</p></div><div><h3>Second probe</h3><p>It introduces “firm culture” before the evaluator has used that explanation.</p><p>The agreement may reflect the question rather than the evaluator's original account.</p></div></div>

<div class="criterion"><strong>Research question:</strong> How do evaluators construct cultural fit? A useful follow-up asks for evidence without supplying the explanation.</div>

---

## Rivera's evidence {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><img class="paper" src="images/rivera_title_crop.png" alt="Title and abstract of Rivera's Hiring as Cultural Matching"><div><p>Rivera interviewed <strong>120 evaluators</strong> in elite professional-service firms and observed one hiring committee.</p><p>The interviews elicited evaluators' criteria and accounts of recently interviewed candidates.</p><p>The committee observation showed how evaluations were produced and contested in real time.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Lauren A. Rivera (2012), “Hiring as Cultural Matching,” <em>American Sociological Review</em> 77(6): 999–1022.</div>

## Life histories and social context {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><img class="paper" src="images/130502235eb69144.jpg" alt="C. R. Shaw student paper describing the case study method"><div><p>Chicago sociologists used interviews and autobiographical accounts to connect a person's experience to institutions and social change.</p><p>The researcher still selected, organized and interpreted the life record.</p><p><strong>Question:</strong> Is one short interview adequate to the timescale and context of the claim?</p><div class="citation">C. R. Shaw student paper, Sociology 353, Ernest Watson Burgess Papers, University of Chicago Library.</div></div></div>

---

## The focused interview {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><img class="paper" src="images/merton_title_crop.png" alt="First page of Merton and Kendall's The Focused Interview"><div><p>Merton and Kendall studied responses to films, broadcasts and experimental situations that the researchers had already analysed.</p><p>That prior analysis gave interviewers questions to pursue. Interviewers still had to leave participants room to describe an unexpected response.</p><p>The methodological problem was how to seek detail without dictating the account.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Robert K. Merton & Patricia L. Kendall (1946), “The Focused Interview,” <em>American Journal of Sociology</em> 51(6): 541–557.</div>

---

## Merton and Kendall's four criteria {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols4060"><div><ol class="large-list"><li>nondirection;</li><li>specificity;</li><li>range;</li><li>depth and personal context.</li></ol><p>They called these criteria provisional and interrelated.</p><p>For them, depth concerned affective significance and personal context.</p></div><img class="source-crop" src="images/merton_criteria_crop.png" alt="Merton and Kendall's four criteria on page 545"></div>

<div class="citation">Merton & Kendall (1946), p. 545.</div>

---

## Specificity without leading {.transcript-slide}

<div class="transcript transcript-wide"><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Response:</span> “I found it uncomfortable.”</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Probe A:</span> “Was there a particular moment when you began to feel uncomfortable?”</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Probe B:</span> “Was it the speaker's dismissive tone that made you uncomfortable?”</div></div>

<div class="cols"><div><h3>Probe A</h3><p>Requests a concrete moment.</p></div><div><h3>Probe B</h3><p>Introduces both a feature and an interpretation.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Instructor-written example based on Merton & Kendall (1946), especially pp. 545–551.</div>

---

## Standardized survey interviewing {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols4060"><img class="paper paper-compact" src="images/fowler_mangione_cover.jpg" alt="Cover of Standardized Survey Interviewing"><div><p><strong>Read questions as written.</strong></p><p><strong>Use agreed clarifications and probes.</strong></p><p><strong>Follow the same skip and coding rules.</strong></p><p>The interviewer's discretion is deliberately restricted because the aim is comparable measurement.</p><div class="citation">Floyd J. Fowler Jr. & Thomas W. Mangione (1990), <em>Standardized Survey Interviewing</em>. SAGE.</div></div></div>

---

## Standardization and clarification {.transcript-slide}

<div class="transcript transcript-wide"><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Interviewer:</span> In the last week, how many times did you exercise?</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Respondent:</span> Does walking to work count?</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Strict response:</span> Whatever exercise means to you.</div><div class="turn"><span class="speaker">Clarification:</span> Count walking if it lasted ten minutes and raised your breathing rate.</div></div>

<p>The strict response preserves identical wording. The clarification may help the respondent use the intended definition, but it changes what this respondent hears.</p>

<div class="citation">Illustrative example based on Schober & Conrad (1997), “Does Conversational Interviewing Reduce Survey Measurement Error?”, <em>Public Opinion Quarterly</em> 61(4): 576–602.</div>

---

## The interviewer has to respond {.transcript-slide}

<div class="repair-question"><span>Respondent</span><p>“Does walking to work count as exercise?”</p></div>

<div class="repair-options"><div><h3>Repeat the question</h3><p>Preserves the wording but leaves the category unclear.</p></div><div><h3>Give the agreed definition</h3><p>Helps the respondent use the intended concept.</p></div><div><h3>Improvise an explanation</h3><p>May help in the moment but creates interviewer variation.</p></div></div>

<div class="repair-record"><strong>Record:</strong> the clarification and the answer that followed it. <strong>Report:</strong> which clarifications interviewers were allowed to give.</div>

<p class="plain-takeaway">A model must make the same kind of decision when a participant asks for help or gives an unclear answer.</p>

<div class="citation">Suchman & Jordan (1990), “Interactional Troubles in Face-to-Face Survey Interviews”; Schober & Conrad (1997).</div>

---

## Oakley on power and reciprocity {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><img class="paper" src="images/oakley_power_crop.png" alt="Oakley's discussion of power and reciprocity"><div><p>Oakley's argument grew from four interviews each with 55 women, from pregnancy to five months after birth.</p><p>Participants asked her hundreds of questions. Conventional advice said that answering could bias the data. Oakley argued that refusing could be exploitative.</p><div class="quote">“The two basic questions were about power and reciprocity.”</div></div></div>

<div class="citation">Ann Oakley (2016), “Interviewing Women Again: Power, Time and the Gift,” <em>Sociology</em> 50(1): 195–213, pp. 197–199.</div>

---

## Bourdieu on the interview relationship {.paper-slide}

<div class="source-highlight-wrap"><img src="images/bourdieu_note2_crop.png" alt="Bourdieu's complete note 2 on questionnaires, interviews and social structures"><div class="highlight-note2" aria-hidden="true"></div></div>

<p>Bourdieu argues that social structures shape both the interaction being studied and the researcher's interaction with the participant.</p>

<div class="citation">Pierre Bourdieu (1996), “Understanding,” <em>Theory, Culture & Society</em> 13(2): 17–37, p. 34, note 2.</div>

---

## Signals of attention {.quote-slide}

<div class="attention-signals"><span>“yes”</span><span>“right”</span><span>a nod</span><span>a look</span><span>a smile</span></div>

<div class="attention-reading"><div><strong>Bourdieu's argument</strong><p>These small responses help the participant continue. Visible inattention can make someone lose the thread.</p></div><div><strong>For an AI interviewer</strong><p>The system can generate acknowledgments and paraphrases. We need to find out whether participants experience them as attention, empty fluency or surveillance.</p></div></div>

<div class="repair-record"><strong>Question for evaluation:</strong> Did the acknowledgment help the participant develop the account, or did it simply make the system sound attentive?</div>

<div class="citation">Bourdieu (1996), note 4 and pp. 17–37.</div>

---

## Accounts and conduct {.transcript-slide}

<div class="quote">“When senior students are in the room, I decide not to speak because I assume their comments will be more sophisticated.”</div>

<div class="evidence-levels"><div><strong>The participant said</strong><p>They worry about intellectual worth.</p></div><div><strong>The account may help explain</strong><p>How they understand participation.</p></div><div><strong>The account alone cannot show</strong><p>That they always remain silent around senior students.</p></div></div>

## The attitudinal fallacy {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><div class="source-highlight-wrap"><img src="images/jerolmack_fallacy_crop.png" alt="Jerolmack and Khan discuss the attitude-behaviour consistency problem and define the attitudinal fallacy"><div class="source-mark highlight-abc" aria-hidden="true"></div><div class="source-mark highlight-fallacy" aria-hidden="true"></div></div><div><p><strong>ABC problem:</strong> verbal responses at one point often fail to predict observed behaviour later.</p><p>Jerolmack and Khan call the unsupported inference from talk to conduct the <strong>attitudinal fallacy</strong>.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Colin Jerolmack & Shamus Khan (2014), “Talk Is Cheap: Ethnography and the Attitudinal Fallacy,” <em>Sociological Methods & Research</em> 43(2): 178–209, p. 179.</div>

---

## LaPiere's study {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><div class="source-highlight-wrap"><img src="images/jerolmack_lapiere_crop.png" alt="Jerolmack and Khan recount LaPiere's study"><div class="source-mark highlight-lapiere" aria-hidden="true"></div></div><div><ol><li>LaPiere travelled with a young Chinese couple in the 1930s.</li><li>They were denied service once in 251 visits.</li><li>Six months later, only one proprietor said they would admit a Chinese guest.</li></ol><p>The survey answers poorly predicted conduct during the earlier encounters.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Jerolmack & Khan (2014), p. 182, discussing LaPiere (1934).</div>

---

## The situation matters {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><div class="source-highlight-wrap"><img src="images/jerolmack_budget_crop.png" alt="Jerolmack and Khan discuss Dean and Whyte's budgeting example"><div class="source-mark highlight-budget-account" aria-hidden="true"></div></div><div><p><strong>In an interview:</strong> a woman endorses careful family budgeting.</p><p><strong>While shopping with a friend:</strong> she buys a dress outside the plan amid social competition.</p><p>Neither setting reveals a single “real” attitude. They are different social situations.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Jerolmack & Khan (2014), p. 183, discussing Dean & Whyte (1958).</div>

---

## What interviews can establish {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><div class="source-highlight-wrap"><img src="images/jerolmack_uses_crop.png" alt="Jerolmack and Khan discuss appropriate uses of interviews"><div class="source-mark highlight-uses-account" aria-hidden="true"></div><div class="source-mark highlight-uses-limit" aria-hidden="true"></div></div><div><h3>Interviews can tell us about</h3><p>Meanings, expectations, retrospective narratives and experiences that cannot be observed directly.</p><h3>Claims about conduct need more</h3><p>Observation, triangulation or evidence that this kind of account predicts the behaviour being claimed.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Jerolmack & Khan (2014), p. 180.</div>

---

## Rivera combines interviews and observation {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><img class="paper" src="images/rivera_methods_crop.png" alt="Rivera's methods sections on interviews and participant observation"><div><p><strong>Interviews:</strong> evaluators explained their criteria, assessed mock résumés and discussed candidates.</p><p><strong>Observation:</strong> a hiring committee showed how candidate evaluations were produced and contested.</p><p>The interview gives us evaluators' accounts. Observation shows part of the decision process outside those accounts.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Rivera (2012), pp. 1004–1005.</div>

---

## What “cultural fit” contained {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><img class="paper" src="images/rivera_figure1_crop.png" alt="Rivera Figure 1 showing processes through which cultural similarities affected evaluation"><div><p>Evaluators used similarity in several ways:</p><ul><li>to sort candidates into a firm type;</li><li>to interpret their answers;</li><li>to generate excitement or connection.</li></ul><p>Asking only whether someone was a good fit would miss these differences.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Rivera (2012), Figure 1 and pp. 1005–1006.</div>

---

## CAPI, CASI and audio-CASI

<p class="bridge-intro">Rivera showed that wording shapes what an interview elicits. Survey researchers also varied who or what presented the question.</p>

<div class="mode3"><div><div class="mode-label">CAPI</div><p>A human reads the question from a computer and enters the answer.</p></div><div><div class="mode-label">CASI</div><p>The participant reads the question and enters the answer privately.</p></div><div><div class="mode-label">Audio-CASI</div><p>The participant hears a recording and answers on the device.</p></div></div>

<p class="plain-takeaway">All three can implement complex branching, but the questions and branches are written in advance.</p>

<div class="citation">Tourangeau & Smith (1996), “Asking Sensitive Questions,” <em>Public Opinion Quarterly</em> 60(2): 275–304.</div>

---

## Tourangeau and Smith on sensitive questions {.paper-slide}

<div class="tourangeau-layout"><div class="tourangeau-window"><img src="images/tourangeau_table3_crop.png" alt="Tourangeau and Smith Table 3"></div><div><p><strong>Study:</strong> 339 adults answered questions about sexual behaviour and drug use using CAPI, CASI or audio-CASI.</p><p><strong>Finding:</strong> audio-CASI produced the highest mean reported number of sex partners.</p><p>Greater disclosure and greater accuracy are separate questions.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Roger Tourangeau & Tom W. Smith (1996), Table 3, pp. 292–293.</div>

---

## Adaptive interviewing with an LLM

Earlier computer-assisted interviews presented questions and branches written in advance.

<div class="crucial">An LLM can write a new follow-up after reading an open-ended answer.</div>

That decision can reflect the research protocol, the preceding conversation and the model's own interpretation of the answer.

After the break: what current studies tell us about AI-assisted and AI-led interviews.

## Three kinds of AI interview

<table class="tbl roomy"><tr><th>Arrangement</th><th>Who chooses the next question?</th><th>What must be recorded?</th></tr><tr><td>AI assistance</td><td>The model suggests. A human interviewer decides.</td><td>Suggestion, human edit and final question.</td></tr><tr><td>Human approval</td><td>The model writes. A human approves or changes it.</td><td>Conversation, output, approval and edit.</td></tr><tr><td>AI-led interview</td><td>The model writes and delivers the question.</td><td>Conversation, model, settings and exact output.</td></tr></table>

---

## How an answer becomes a follow-up question

<div class="flow"><div><strong>Protocol</strong><br>research aim and required topics</div><div><strong>Conversation</strong><br>questions and answers so far</div><div><strong>Model call</strong><br>instructions plus conversation</div><div><strong>Question</strong><br>generated follow-up</div><div><strong>Record</strong><br>input, output and any edit</div></div>

<p class="plain-takeaway">Reconstructing the exchange requires the conversation sent to the model and the question it returned.</p>

---

## Personalized persuasion after an AI interview {.paper-slide}

<div class="velez-intro"><img src="images/velez_liu_clifford_title_abstract.png" alt="Title and abstract of Beyond Belief Change"><div><p><strong>Question:</strong> Do arguments change attitudes more when they address a belief the participant regards as central?</p><p>Participants discussed a political position with an LLM.</p><p>The model summarized their position, identified a focal belief and generated a relevant belief they had not mentioned.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Yamil Ricardo Velez, Patrick Liu & Scott Clifford (2026), “Beyond Belief Change,” <em>American Political Science Review</em>.</div>

---

## How the model classified the interview {.paper-slide}

<img class="velez-table" src="images/velez_liu_clifford_table2_example.png" alt="Published Table 2 example showing the interview and generated belief measures">

<div class="cols"><div><p><strong>Focal belief:</strong> a reason expressed in the conversation and treated as central to the attitude.</p></div><div><p><strong>Distal belief:</strong> a relevant reason generated by the model but not mentioned by the participant.</p></div></div>

<div class="criterion">Does the focal-belief statement represent the conversation accurately?</div>

<div class="citation">Velez, Liu & Clifford (2026), Table 2.</div>

---

## The three experimental conditions {.paper-slide}

<img class="velez-flow" src="images/velez_liu_clifford_figure2_bottom.png" alt="Published Figure 2 showing random assignment and post-treatment measures">

<p class="plain-takeaway">Participants received a counterargument aimed at the focal belief, a counterargument aimed at the generated distal belief, or a placebo message.</p>

<div class="citation">Velez, Liu & Clifford (2026), Figure 2.</div>

---

## Focal-belief messages had larger effects {.paper-slide}

<div class="velez-result"><img src="images/velez_liu_clifford_figure7.png" alt="Published Figure 7 comparing effects of focal and distal counterarguments"><div><p>Positive values favour the focal-belief condition.</p><p><strong>Overall difference:</strong> 0.054 control-group standard deviations (<em>p</em> = .014).</p><p>Eleven of twelve comparisons favoured the focal-belief condition, although several estimates were imprecise.</p><p>Each interview summary requires separate validation.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Velez, Liu & Clifford (2026), Figure 7 and pp. 14–15.</div>

---

## Text and voice interviews {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><img class="paper" src="images/geiecke_title_abstract_crop.png" alt="Title and abstract of Conversations at Scale by Geiecke and Jaravel"><div><p>Geiecke and Jaravel compare human and AI interviewers, text and voice input, prompts and models.</p><p>The comparisons distinguish design choices that are often bundled together as “AI interviewing.”</p><p>Their platform sends the system instruction and conversation back to the model after each answer.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Friedrich Geiecke & Xavier Jaravel (2026), “Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-led Interviews,” working paper.</div>

---

## Voice architecture in Geiecke and Jaravel {.paper-slide}

<img class="voice-source" src="images/geiecke_voice_architecture_crop.png" alt="Published description and technical footnote for the Geiecke and Jaravel voice interview setup">

<div class="voice-route"><div><span>1</span><strong>Participant</strong><p>Speaks into the microphone.</p></div><div><span>2</span><strong>Whisper</strong><p>Transcribes the answer.</p></div><div><span>3</span><strong>GPT-4o audio</strong><p>Returns text and spoken audio.</p></div><div><span>4</span><strong>Coral voice</strong><p>Delivers the next question.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Geiecke & Jaravel (2026), section 3.4.2 and note 43. Their system used <code>gpt-4o-audio-preview-2024-12-17</code>.</div>

---

## Spoken answers received higher grades {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols4060"><div><p>Eight sociology PhD students graded transcripts against what a human expert might achieve.</p><p>Using the same prompt and GPT-4o, the mean grade was:</p><p class="result-number">2.82 <span>typed</span><br>3.63 <span>spoken</span></p><p>The authors argue that speech produced more information and supported more precise follow-up.</p></div><img class="paper" src="images/geiecke_table3_panel_a.png" alt="Table III Panel A comparing text and voice input"></div>

<div class="citation">Geiecke & Jaravel (2026), Table III, Panel A. Thirty transcripts per condition.</div>

---

## Human and AI interviewers {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols6040"><img class="paper" src="images/wuttke_design_crop.png" alt="Wuttke study design"><div><p>Participants discussed politics and democracy with an AI interviewer or a student interviewer.</p><p>The AI used GPT-4 Turbo. Participants could choose text or voice.</p><p>The study included five AI-led and six human-led interviews, so the comparison is exploratory.</p></div></div>

<div class="citation">Alexander Wuttke et al. (2025), “AI Conversational Interviewing,” <em>LaTeCH-CLfL 2025</em>: 132–144.</div>

---

## Different interviewer errors

<div class="cols"><div><h3>AI interviewer</h3><ul><li>missed surprising or unclear answers;</li><li>sometimes praised or evaluated responses;</li><li>produced long turns and suffered latency or transcription problems.</li></ul></div><div><h3>Student interviewers</h3><ul><li>more often failed to show active listening;</li><li>sometimes guided the answer;</li><li>were not an expert-interviewer benchmark.</li></ul></div></div>

<p class="plain-takeaway">The eleven-interview sample maps possible errors. The sample is too small to rank the two interviewer types.</p>

<div class="citation">Wuttke et al. (2025), pp. 137–140 and Table 1.</div>

---

## Fixed and adaptive probes {.paper-slide}

<img class="wide" src="images/cuevas_figure2.png" alt="Cuevas Figure 2 showing assignment to baseline, Dynamic Prober and Member Checker conditions">

<div class="citation">Cuevas et al. (2025), Figure 2, “Collecting Social Data with Large Language Models,” <em>PACM HCI</em>.</div>

---

## Cuevas and colleagues' three conditions

<table class="tbl"><tr><th>Condition</th><th>After each main answer</th><th>At the end</th></tr><tr><td><strong>Fixed baseline</strong></td><td>Asked “Can you elaborate?” and “Can you provide an example?”</td><td>Ended the conversation.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Dynamic Prober</strong></td><td>GPT-3.5 Turbo wrote two follow-up questions.</td><td>Ended the conversation.</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Dynamic Prober and Member Checker</strong></td><td>Used the same generated follow-ups.</td><td>Generated a summary the participant could confirm or contest.</td></tr></table>

<p class="plain-takeaway">The study assigned 399 participants and collected 4,308 open-ended responses.</p>

<div class="citation">Cuevas et al. (2025), sections 3.3, 4.2, 5 and Appendix D.</div>

---

## Better follow-up, but little evidence of greater depth {.paper-slide}

<div class="cols4060"><div><p>The Dynamic Prober improved the follow-up score.</p><p>Across most other quality measures, the adaptive conditions resembled the fixed baseline.</p><p>Answers were usually clear and relevant, but often lacked specific examples and the participant's perspective.</p></div><img class="paper evidence-figure" src="images/cuevas_figure5_crop.png" alt="Cuevas Figure 5 comparing quality and richness indicators"></div>

<div class="citation">Cuevas et al. (2025), Figure 5 and sections 6–8.</div>

---

## When the bot claimed to enjoy the interview {.quote-slide}

The Member Checker used friendly language after the interview. One participant objected:

<div class="quote quote-large">“Clearly, it didn’t ‘enjoy’ anything, and saying so felt manipulative.”</div>

The comment shows how this participant interpreted the relationship performed by the chatbot. It also returns us to Oakley's question about reciprocity and the obligations created by an interview.

<div class="citation">Cuevas et al. (2025), p. 14.</div>

## Worked example: Rivera's hiring interview

<div class="interview-brief"><div class="brief-aim"><span>Research question</span><p>How do evaluators decide that a candidate is a good cultural fit?</p></div><div class="brief-opener"><span>Opening question</span><p>Tell me about a recent candidate who seemed like a good fit for the firm.</p></div><div class="brief-rule"><span>Rule for the next question</span><p>Ask for a concrete judgment, episode or comparison. Do not name class background, similarity or another cause unless the evaluator has already done so.</p></div></div>

<div class="model-output"><span>Evaluator's first answer</span><p>I could picture her working here.</p></div>

---

## Exercise 1: interviewer advice {.tight-code}

```python
research_question = (
    "How do evaluators decide that a candidate "
    "is a good cultural fit?"
)
interviewer_advice = (
    "Ask one short follow-up that requests a concrete example. "
    "Do not suggest a cause or answer for the evaluator."
)
first_answer = "Evaluator: I could picture her working here."
```

<div class="io-strip"><div><strong>Researcher input</strong><br><code>interviewer_advice</code> is an editable string.</div><div><strong>Interview input</strong><br><code>first_answer</code> contains the evaluator's exact words.</div></div>

---

## The model receives the advice {.tight-code}

```python
interviewer_messages = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": (
            f"Research question: {research_question}\n"
            f"Advice for the interviewer: {interviewer_advice}\n"
            "Return only the next interview question."
        ),
    },
    {"role": "user", "content": first_answer},
]
```

<p>The <code>f</code> before the string inserts the current research question and advice.</p>

---

## Generate the probe with OpenRouter {.tight-code}

```python
with OpenRouter(
    api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]
) as client:
    interviewer_response = client.chat.send(
        model=HOSTED_MODEL,
        messages=interviewer_messages,
        temperature=0,
    )

interviewer_raw = interviewer_response.choices[0].message.content
```

---

## Generate the probe with Ollama {.tight-code}

```python
interviewer_response = ollama.chat(
    think=False,
    model=LOCAL_MODEL,
    messages=interviewer_messages,
    options={"temperature": 0},
)

interviewer_raw = interviewer_response.message.content
interviewer_probe = interviewer_raw.strip()
print("Generated probe:", interviewer_probe)
```

---

## Tinker with the interviewer advice {.transcript-slide}

<div class="path-compare"><div><div class="pair-label">Request an example</div><p>Ask for a concrete episode. Do not name a cause in advance.</p></div><div><div class="pair-label">Request a comparison</div><p>Ask how this candidate differed from one who did not seem to fit.</p></div></div>

<div class="model-output"><span>Change one string</span><p>Edit <code>interviewer_advice</code>, rebuild <code>interviewer_messages</code>, and generate another probe.</p></div>

<p class="plain-takeaway">The advice can change what the model pursues and what assumptions enter the interview.</p>

---

## Exercise 2: a fictional interviewee {.tight-code}

```python
persona = {
    "role": "junior evaluator at a consulting firm",
    "decision_power": "takes notes but has no final vote",
    "evaluation_style": "prefers evidence from the case exercise",
    "known_episode": (
        "the candidate challenged a case assumption calmly"
    ),
}

print(persona["role"])
```

<p>The dictionary contains details supplied by the researcher. It does not describe a real or representative evaluator.</p>

---

## The persona becomes model input {.tight-code}

```python
persona_text = json.dumps(persona, indent=2)
persona_messages = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": (
            "Generate fictional test data. Use only the supplied "
            "persona details and say when the persona does not know."
        ),
    },
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": (
            f"Fictional persona:\n{persona_text}\n\n"
            f"Interview question:\n{interviewer_probe}"
        ),
    },
]
```

<p>The output of Exercise 1 becomes part of the input to Exercise 2.</p>

---

## Generate the fictional answer with OpenRouter {.tight-code}

```python
if ROUTE == "openrouter":
    with OpenRouter(api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) as client:
        synthetic_response = client.chat.send(
            model=HOSTED_MODEL,
            messages=persona_messages,
            temperature=0,
    )
    synthetic_raw = synthetic_response.choices[0].message.content
```

<p><code>persona_messages</code> is the input. <code>synthetic_response</code> is the complete SDK response object. The final line retrieves the returned text.</p>

---

## Generate the fictional answer with Ollama {.tight-code}

```python
else:
    synthetic_response = ollama.chat(think=False,
        model=LOCAL_MODEL,
        messages=persona_messages,
        options={"temperature": 0},
    )
    synthetic_raw = synthetic_response.message.content

synthetic_answer = synthetic_raw.strip()
print("Synthetic answer:", synthetic_answer)
```

<p>Both routes produce the same Python variable: <code>synthetic_answer</code>. This lets the rest of the notebook work in the same way whichever route was selected.</p>

---

## What the synthetic answer is for

<table class="tbl roomy"><tr><th>It can help us inspect</th><th>It cannot establish</th></tr><tr><td>Whether the question is intelligible</td><td>How real evaluators understand cultural fit</td></tr><tr><td>Whether the question invites an invented detail</td><td>How frequently an answer would occur</td></tr><tr><td>Whether a different persona changes the answer</td><td>Whether the persona represents a social group</td></tr></table>

<p class="plain-takeaway">Here the persona provides test material for an interview protocol. Week 7 asks what would be required to use synthetic answers as population evidence.</p>

---

## The interview has to keep an ordered history {.tight-code}

```python
conversation = [{"role": "user", "content": first_answer}]
conversation.append({"role": "assistant", "content": interviewer_probe})
conversation.append({"role": "user", "content": synthetic_answer})

print(len(conversation))
print(conversation[1]["content"])
```

<div class="io-strip"><div><strong><code>conversation[1]</code></strong><br>Select the second turn.</div><div><strong><code>["content"]</code></strong><br>Select the text stored inside that turn.</div></div>

<p class="plain-takeaway">The model does not remember the earlier call by itself. The program sends the relevant history again.</p>

---

## Save the advice, persona and conversation {.tight-code}

```python
research_record = {
    "route": ROUTE,
    "interviewer_advice": interviewer_advice,
    "persona": persona,
    "conversation": conversation,
}

print(json.dumps(research_record, indent=2))
```

## Before using an AI interview transcript

1. What is the interview supposed to tell us?
2. What choices could the interviewer or model make?
3. How might the interview itself affect the answer?
4. What evidence supports the final claim?
